extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students studying real analysis (Math 104) or readers following Rudin
extracted.subtask_description: Lecture notes for a first course in real analysis following Rudin: introduces number systems, topology of R, sequences/series, continuity, differentiation, Riemann integral, uniform convergence and related theorems. Designed as a course reference for proofs, definitions, and standard theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: ℚ is a field
rubrics_metrics.description: (Proposition 1.1) (ℚ, +, ⋅) is a field: (ℚ, +) is an abelian group with identity 0; ℚ is closed under addition; addition associative; additive identity 0; additive inverses exist; addition commutative. (ℚ, +, ⋅) is a commutative unital ring: ℚ closed under multiplication; multiplication associative; multiplicative identity 1; multiplication commutative; distributive law holds. Any nonzero element has multiplicative inverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit list of algebraic axioms illustrated on ℚ; example that ℤ is ring but not field (no multiplicative inverses for many elements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordered set
rubrics_metrics.description: (Definition 1.3) A set X with order ≺ satisfies: for any a,b ∈ X exactly one of a ≺ b, b ≺ a, or a = b; transitivity: if a ≺ b and b ≺ c then a ≺ c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: define ≺ on ℚ by a ≺ b iff a−b negative (i.e., usual <). Also note subsets of ordered sets inherit order; partial orders example (2ℤ, ⊂) is only partial order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordered field (compatibility of order and field operations)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Definition 1.8) A field (X,+,⋅) is an ordered field if order ≺ satisfies: (1) if x ≺ y then x+z ≺ y+z for all z; (2) if 0 ≺ x and 0 ≺ y then 0 ≺ x⋅y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows ℚ with < is an ordered field; stresses compatibility required between algebraic and order structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper/lower bounds and sup/inf (least upper bound / greatest lower bound)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Definitions 1.9,1.11) Upper bound: x ∈ X with a ≤ x for all a in S. Least upper bound (supremum): smallest upper bound. Analogous definitions for lower bound and infimum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sup of (1,2] is 2 and is max; sup of sets in ℚ may fail to exist (e.g., {x∈ℚ|x^2 ≤ 2} has no sup in ℚ). Uniqueness of sup/inf if they exist (Lemma 1.12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Least-upper-bound (l.u.b.) property / completeness axiom
rubrics_metrics.description: (Definition 1.14) An ordered set (X,≺) satisfies the least-upper-bound property if any nonempty subset with an upper bound has a least upper bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This property fails for ℚ and motivates construction of ℝ. Equivalent to greatest-lower-bound property (exercise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of ℝ via Dedekind cuts
rubrics_metrics.description: (Section 2.1) Real numbers are defined as Dedekind cuts: subsets C of ℚ satisfying (a) C ≠ ∅, C ≠ ℚ; (b) if c∈C and x<c then x∈C; (c) if c∈C then ∃x>c with x∈C. ℝ is the set of all such cuts, ordered by ⊂.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties: ℝ ordered by ⊂, addition defined on cuts C1+C2={x1+x2|x1∈C1,x2∈C2}; multiplication definable; (ℝ,+,⋅) is a field and an ordered field and satisfies l.u.b. property. Map F:q ↦ {x∈ℚ|x<q} injects ℚ into cuts. Exercises showing cuts not coming from ℚ (e.g., set {x∈ℚ|x<0 or x^2≤2}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Archimedean property
rubrics_metrics.description: (Theorem 2.3 / Proposition 2.4) For any x∈ℝ+ and y∈ℝ there exists n∈ℤ+ with n⋅x>y. In particular, for any y∈ℝ there exists positive integer n>y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses l.u.b. property: otherwise ℤ+ would have an upper bound contradicting minimality argument. Remark: archimedean property allows decimal representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Density of ℚ in ℝ
rubrics_metrics.description: (Theorem 2.6) For any a<b in ℝ there exists x∈ℚ with a<x<b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to finding integers m,n with a n < m < b n using archimedean property and lemma that if β−α>1 there is an integer between α and β (Lemma 2.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure of ℝ under taking roots
rubrics_metrics.description: (Theorem 2.8) For every y∈ℝ+ and n∈ℤ+ there exists a unique x∈ℝ+ with x^n = y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniqueness follows from ordered field properties; existence via set S={a∈ℝ+|a^n<y} and taking sup S, showing sup^n = y by l.u.b. arguments. Notation y^{1/n}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended real number system
rubrics_metrics.description: (Section 2.5) ℝ ∪ {±∞} is the extended real number system: sup S = +∞ if S has no upper bound; inf S = −∞ if S has no lower bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operations with ±∞ can be defined formally but ℝ∪{±∞} is not a field. Advantage: every nonempty subset of ℝ has sup/inf in extended system.

rubrics_metrics.name: ℝ^2 as Euclidean plane (vector space, inner product, norm)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Section 3) ℝ^2 = ℝ×ℝ with componentwise addition and scalar multiplication; inner product ⟨(x1,x2),(y1,y2)⟩ = x1y1+x2y2. Induced norm |x| = sqrt(x1^2+x2^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties listed: positivity, homogeneity |c x| = |c||x|, triangle inequality |x+y| ≤ |x|+|y|, Cauchy-Schwarz |⟨x,y⟩| ≤ |x||y|. Generalizes to ℝ^n. Multiplication on ℝ^2 defined to give ℂ via (a,b)(c,d)=(ac−bd,ad+bc).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex numbers ℂ as a field
rubrics_metrics.description: (Section 4) Identify ℝ^2 with ℂ by (x,y)↦x+iy and impose i^2=−1; (ℂ,+,⋅) is a field. For z=x+iy, real part x, imaginary part y, norm |z|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard identification and field structure; notes ℂ is uncountable as ℝ is uncountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countable vs uncountable sets
rubrics_metrics.description: (Chapter 2, §1) Definitions: finite sets; countable sets (∞ set X is countable if ℤ+ ∼ X); uncountable sets (not countable). Examples: ℤ+, ℤ, ℚ are countable; ℝ, ℂ are uncountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propositions: bijection is an equivalence relation; Cartesian products of countable sets are countable (Prop 1.6); any subset of countable set is at most countable (Prop 1.7). Cantor diagonal argument used to show certain infinite products are uncountable (Prop 1.11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric space
rubrics_metrics.description: (Definition 2.2) A metric space is a set X with d:X×X→ℝ satisfying: (1) d(x,y)≥0 and d(x,y)=0 iff x=y; (2) symmetry d(x,y)=d(y,x); (3) triangle inequality d(x,z) ≤ d(x,y)+d(y,z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (ℝ, d) with d(x,y)=|x−y|; (ℝ^2,d) with Euclidean distance. Metrics induce metrics on subsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open and closed sets (in metric spaces)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Definitions 2.3,2.5) Open ball Br(x) = {y|d(y,x)<r}. A set S⊂X is open if for every x∈S ∃r>0 with Br(x)⊂S. A set is closed if its complement is open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties: ∅ and X open/closed; finite intersections and arbitrary unions of open sets are open (Prop 2.7), dually unions/intersections for closed sets (Prop 2.11). Examples: intervals in ℝ, open/closed balls. Counterexamples illustrating infinite intersections/unions behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit points, closure, and dense sets
rubrics_metrics.description: (Definition 2.13 & 2.15) x is a limit point of S if every neighborhood of x intersects S at a point ≠ x. Closure S̄ = S ∪ S'. S is dense if S̄ = X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propositions: closure is closed and is smallest closed superset (Prop 2.16–2.18). Relation with sequences: x is limit point of S iff ∃ sequence x_n ∈ S\\{x} with x_n→x (Prop 2.22). Examples: ℚ dense in ℝ; closure of (a,b] is [a,b].

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence of sequences in metric spaces and uniqueness of limits
rubrics_metrics.description: (Definition 2.19, Lemma 2.21) A sequence x_n converges to x if d(x_n,x)→0. Limits are unique in metric spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs: uniqueness by triangle inequality. Example: 1/n→0 in ℝ by Archimedean property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compactness (open cover definition) and sequential compactness
rubrics_metrics.description: (Definitions 3.1,3.4,3.7 and Theorem 3.8) A set K⊂X is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover. K is sequentially compact if every sequence in K has a convergent subsequence with limit in K. In metric spaces compact ⇔ sequentially compact (Theorem 3.8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: compact sets are closed and bounded (Prop 3.9). Examples and counterexamples for open covers; finite sets are compact. Heine-Borel-type results appear in contents (Heine-Borel theorem referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundedness
rubrics_metrics.description: (Definition 3.2) A subset S of X is bounded if ∃C>0 and x0∈X s.t. d(x,x0) < C for all x∈S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in proving compact ⇒ bounded and in examples distinguishing compactness in ℝ vs general metric spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic sequence and series convergence criteria (chapter contents)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Chapter 3 contents) Sequences: convergence, Cauchy sequences, upper/lower limits. Series: definition and basic properties, comparison test, root and ratio tests, addition and multiplication of series, rearrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists the standard battery of convergence tests to be applied to real or complex series; rearrangement warns about conditional convergence issues (section present in contents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence of functions
rubrics_metrics.description: (Definition 1.1, Chapter 7) A sequence f_n on X converges uniformly to f if ∀ε>0 ∃N independent of x s.t. |f_n(x)−f(x)|<ε for all x∈X and n>N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterization: ε_n := sup_x |f_n(x)−f(x)| → 0 (Theorem 1.3). Cauchy criterion for uniform convergence (Theorem 1.4) and technique to disprove uniform convergence by finding ε0>0 and x_n with |f_nk(x_nk)−f(x_nk)|≥ε0. Examples: x^n on [0,1] converges pointwise but not uniformly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy criterion and Weierstrass M-test for uniform convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: (Theorem 1.4, Theorem 1.5) A sequence f_n uniformly converges iff it is uniformly Cauchy. If |a_n(x)| ≤ M_n for all x and ΣM_n converges, then Σa_n(x) converges uniformly (Weierstrass M-test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate tools for proving uniform convergence of function series and power series on compact subintervals (Theorem 1.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence preserves continuity and related limit interchange
rubrics_metrics.description: (Theorem 2.1, Corollary 2.2) If f_n→f uniformly on S and each f_n has a limit as x→x0, then limits commute: lim_{n→∞} lim_{x→x0} f_n(x) = lim_{x→x0} lim_{n→∞} f_n(x). In particular, uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses uniform Cauchy property and triangle inequality. Application: C0(X) with sup norm is complete (Theorem 2.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: C0(X) completeness and equicontinuity / Arzelà–Ascoli lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: (Theorem 2.3, Definition 2.4, Theorem 2.6) The space C0(X) of continuous real-valued functions on compact X is complete with sup norm. A family F⊂C0(X) is equicontinuous if ∀ε ∃δ independent of f such that d_X(x,y)<δ ⇒ |f(x)−f(y)|<ε. Arzelà–Ascoli: on compact X, any uniformly bounded equicontinuous sequence has a uniformly convergent subsequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates compactness criteria in function spaces; corollary: bounded closed equicontinuous subsets of C0(X) are (sequentially) compact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence and Riemann integration
rubrics_metrics.description: (Theorem 3.1, Corollary 3.2) If f_n ∈ R(α)[a,b] and f_n → f uniformly, then f∈R(α)[a,b] and lim_{n→∞} ∫_a^b f_n dα = ∫_a^b f dα. For a uniformly convergent series of integrable terms, termwise integration is allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate via sup-norm error ε_n and bound integrals by 2 ε_n (α(b)−α(a)); gives justification for integrating power series term-by-term (example: ∫ e^x from power series).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence and differentiation (termwise differentiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Theorem 4.1, Corollary 4.2) If f_n differentiable on [a,b], f_n(x0) converge at some x0, and f_n' converge uniformly on [a,b], then f_n converge uniformly to some differentiable f with f'(x)=lim_{n→∞} f_n'(x). For series: if Σa_n'(x) converges uniformly and Σa_n(x0) converges at some x0, then Σa_n(x) converges to f and f' = Σa_n'(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses mean value theorem and Cauchy/uniform arguments. Example: differentiability of e^x via termwise differentiation of its power series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stone–Weierstrass (Weierstrass) approximation theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: (Theorem 5.1) For any f∈C0([a,b]) there exists a sequence of polynomials P_n uniformly converging to f on [a,b].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch: use Landau kernel Q_n(t)=c_n(1−t^2)^n with ∫_{−1}^1 Q_n = 1 and define P_n = f * Q_n (convolution), each P_n a polynomial and P_n → f uniformly. Notes this theorem's practical/theoretical relevance (polynomial approximation/interpolation).
